comment: Rules for `node scripts/test.js --changed`: the plans a change runs. Both kinds are applied to every changed file. A directory rule (`directoryRules`) looks the path up under test/plans/feat and names the deepest plan directory or plan file that mirrors it (modules/tensor/ops.cpp -> feat/modules/tensor, test/cases/compile/enum/x.cml -> feat/compile/enum.plan.toml). A file rule (`rules`) then adds the plans outside that mirrored tree that the same change can also break (modules/tiles -> test/plans/gpu/tiles*, modules/onnx -> the exporter in feat/trans); the first matching file rule applies to a file, so keep them from specific to general. A rule entry is a path under test/plans, or { "plan": path, "layer": true }: a layered plan stays a named target but follows `--tier` like a directory, so the slow cases an ordinary change must not run (the PyTorch comparisons of autodiff and onnx) are filtered while the fast cases still run; `"layer": true` on the rule is the default for all its entries. A rule with "self": true selects the changed plan file itself (editing a plan runs that plan), except for the paths in "except": those fall back to the fast layer instead of running perf, GC stress, progen or PyTorch. A change no rule matches (or whose plans cannot be found) falls back to the whole fast layer; `--changed --list` prints the selection without running it. The base branch is origin/develop; CAMEL_TEST_BASE overrides it. Deliberately not selectable: test/plans/perf/**, the GC-stress plans (feat/mm/gc*, gpu/tiles_regions, gpu/tiles_decorator) and progen (feat/opt/progen.plan.toml) -- the project forbids those on a shared host, so a change there runs the fast layer and the report says so instead of wiring them in. Update this file when a subsystem grows a plan of its own; see docs/test-plans.md, 'Selecting plans from a change'.

directoryRules.comment: A test case: its directory is looked up under test/plans/feat (compile, linear, modules/tensor, modules/nn.plan.toml, tools/unicode -> tools, ...).
A module: modules/tensor selects feat/modules/tensor, modules/nn selects feat/modules/nn.plan.toml. A module with no plan of its own (python) falls through to the file rules.
A tool: tools/lsp selects feat/tools/lsp.plan.toml; tools/format falls through to the file rules (feat/format).

rules.comment: The runner itself and the self-test: the plans that exercise the runner and the smoke set.
FastVM and the other schedulers.

The optimization passes and the rewrite rule library they run: the opt plans, the pass dumps that print their effect, and the rewrite-rule plan. stdlib/rules.cml is the data these passes run, so it selects the same set. `feat/opt` is a directory target, so `--tier fast` keeps its fast plans and filters the slow progen plan (progen is never selected by a rule).
The profiler pass: its own plan runs without a CUDA device (the host fallback), so it is safe from an ordinary change.
The other translation passes: the graph printers, the C++ emitter, the JSON dump.
The test-only passes (test::facts, test::regions, test::rules, ...): the plans that name them in their arguments.
Any other pass, including the shared pass machinery.
GCT/GIR construction, encoding and the graph printer.
The front end: lexer, parser, AST and diagnostics.
Values, types, the collector and the runtime shell.
Execution, entry arguments and the standalone bridge.

Tiles: the CPU plan, the three GPU plans H154 first ran (all slow, so they are named as plan files and run in full even under --tier fast), the profile plan, and the DDPM plan whose training cases are written against tiles. The GPU plans are what no directory rule could reach before H161.

The ONNX exporter. `layer` is true because the plan's four slow cases are ONNX Runtime and PyTorch comparisons: under --tier fast the fast exporter tests run and those are filtered; --tier all runs them. `feat/trans` holds the dumps that print the exported graph.
Neural-network operators: the nn plan and the plans that train with them.
Automatic differentiation. `layer` is true because five slow cases compare gradients against PyTorch: --tier fast runs the fast autodiff cases and filters those.
Tensor operators and shapes: the tensor plans, the index/operator semantics plans, and autodiff (layered, for the same PyTorch reason), because a shape or operator change shows up in gradients.
Keyed random: the random plan (named, so its slow std::cpp comparison runs) and the registry that lists it.
Graph values and passes, and the rewrite rules built on them.
Checkpoint trees.
I/O: the module's plan and the std facade that wraps it.
JSON values: the accessor/typed/value plans and the std facade.
Bytes and the std facade over them.
Parallel operators: the para plans and the registry that lists their signatures.
The Python bridge: the std plan whose python cases run it and the two consistency plans that drive it.
Numeric operators: the std facade and the operator-semantics plan.
The declaration modules with no plan of their own: their cases live under test/cases/modules/std, which feat/modules/std.plan.toml runs, and their signatures are checked by the registry plan.
Any other module. A directory target, so --tier fast filters the slow cases; a module that grows a specific rule above stops using this one.
The standard library's Camel sources and signatures.
The language server, debugger, formatter and command-line tools.
Example programs and their recorded output.
Documentation checks.
The editor syntax files and their tests.
The build definitions: every backend may be affected, so the smoke set and the runtime plans.
Case directories with no plan directory of their own: their cases are exercised by the module, tool and translation plans.
A case directory with no plan directory of its own: the loop cases are tested by the linear plan.

A plan file selects itself: editing the tests of one plan runs that plan. The except list keeps the plans the project forbids from an ordinary change out of that: a perf, GC-stress or progen plan edit falls back to the fast layer (name the plan file to run it deliberately).
